title: When does rotor cant pay on a small quadrotor co-designed with its motors and controller?
lede: research programme: fixed rotor cant on a co-designed quadrotor; milestone 1 checks the earlier projects' torque limits against a full four-rotor allocation: yaw authority was understated 2–2.8×, yet cant still cuts attitude error by 4.8° (5 of 5 seeds); the TWR-5 optimum of the earlier work does not survive
summary: An open research programme (target IEEE RA-L) on when a fixed rotor cant angle pays on a small quadrotor once arm, propeller, motor headroom and attitude controller are designed with it. It gathers seven earlier simulated steps (codesign-aero-cant to -poshold). Milestone 1 builds the full thrust-to-wrench map of a canted X quadrotor with every rotor thrust bounded and finds, by linear programme (closed forms agree to 1e-15), that the torque limits those steps used understate yaw authority by 2× to 2.8×, overstate roll authority above thrust-to-weight 2 and make the side force √2 too large. Rerunning their joint CMA-ES co-design (1920 evaluations, 5 seeds, 64 held-out episodes, propeller torque ratio from measured UIUC data) with corrected limits: cant up to 35° still beats no cant by 4.81° RMS (5 of 5 seeds; 4.62° before) and the chosen cant stays at 35–37°, but that plateau comes from an attitude-only objective (the canted design weighs 3.17 against 1.74 kg and needs 1.35× the ideal hover power). The earlier interior optimum near TWR 5 disappears: with altitude held the optimiser picks TWR 2.0–2.3. Simulated; mass, cost and motor fits and plant ranges are inherited assumptions; per-axis torque box; no hardware.
